radar.title: The Virtual Biotech: A multi-agent AI framework for therapeutic discovery and development
radar.summary: Drug development requires evidence integration across biological scales and modalities, but relevant tools are fragmented. We introduce the Virtual Biotech, an organization of artificial intelligence (AI) agents modeled on a drug-development company, with agentic divisions spanning target discovery, safety assessment, modality selection, and clinical development. We demonstrate its utility at three drug-development decision points. First, more than 37,000 agents annotated outcomes from 55,984 trials and found that drugs targeting cell type–specific genes were 48% more likely to reach market with 32% fewer adverse events. Second, it integrated multimodal evidence to propose a therapeutic strategy in lung cancer. Third, it analyzed a terminated ulcerative colitis trial and inferred potential mechanisms of failure. These results demonstrate that human-guided multi-agent systems can conduct transparent, multiscale analyses to inform therapeutic-development decisions.

radar.title: Reusability report: multi-sample omics network inference operates in distinct robustness regimes defined by prior knowledge and data availability
radar.summary: Abstract Knowledge-constrained network inference enables the reconstruction of regulatory programmes from high-dimensional biological data, yet the conditions under which shared and context-specific structures can be reliably identified remain poorly understood. Pablo Rodriguez-Mier et al. recently introduced CORNETO, a framework for multi-sample constrained inference. Here we reproduce, evaluate and extend CORNETO in terms of robustness, identifiability and bias–variance trade-offs. Using dynamic haematopoiesis and stable cortical datasets, we systematically assess four network reconstruction paradigms while preserving the original method-specific evaluation procedures and benchmark definitions. We show that multi-sample inference generally improves robustness and reproducibility, although gains in predictive performance depend on biological context and the completeness of the prior network. To enhance stability, we introduce bootstrap aggregation and selective re-expansion strategies that improve consensus robustness and recovery while preserving context-specific signals without modifying the underlying optimization scheme or sacrificing generality. Across datasets and methods, our results reveal distinct inference regimes governed by sample availability, prior knowledge and regularization. Together, these findings position network reconstruction as a regime-dependent learning problem and provide practical principles for robust multi-sample biological network inference.

radar.title: dITP shifts the assembly equilibrium of Kongming to activate NAD+ hydrolysis
radar.summary: Abstract The Kongming (Kom) system, consisting of KomA, KomB, and KomC, protects bacteria from phage infection. KomA collaborates with a phage enzyme to generate deoxyinosine 5′-triphosphate (dITP), which activates the KomBC complex to hydrolyze NAD⁺ and trigger cell death. Recent studies propose that dITP activates KomBC through a simple conformational change. Our findings instead reveal a more dynamic mechanism. Without dITP, KomBC complexes exist in equilibrium between tightly packed oligomers and loosely packed filaments, both inactive. Tight packing accumulates unfavorable electrostatic interactions without positioning catalytic residues for NAD⁺ hydrolysis, whereas loose packing relieves these interactions but leaves catalytic residues misaligned. dITP binding at KomB stabilizes tightly packed KomC cores in the filament while aligning catalytic residues. Therefore, a small-molecule signal activates signaling by shifting the assembly equilibrium of higher-order protein complexes toward a catalytically competent state.

radar.title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Environment for Beyond-Visual-Range Air Combat
radar.summary: An open simulation environment is presented for training multiple reinforcement-learning agents in beyond-visual-range air combat while balancing physical fidelity against rollout speed. The objective is to provide a reproducible testbed that retains the sensing, tracking, weapon, and cooperative-information effects governing long-range engagements without the computational cost of a full mission simulator. Aircraft and missiles use geodetic four-degree-of-freedom kinematics and energy-based aerodynamics; probabilistic radar detections, electronic-warfare effects, shared-track fusion, seeker-constrained missile guidance, and distance-dependent terminal lethality are represented explicitly. Fixed-shape observations and safety-gated actions support parallel self-play. End-to-end experiments with a memoryless policy learned boundary compliance, survival, and progressively more effective weapon employment, while subsystem profiling measured approximately ten seconds of wall-clock time for a 300-step two-versus-two episode on the reported hardware. These results establish internal training readiness and reproducible computational scaling and form a platform for reproducible research on learned tactics and fair benchmarking in this domain.
radar.summary_short: An open simulation environment is presented for training multiple reinforcement-learning agents in beyond-visual-range air combat while balancing physical fidelity against rollout speed.

radar.title: Multiagent Assortment Optimization in Sequential Matching Markets
radar.summary: Motivated by the challenges faced by choice-based matching platforms, in this work, we study a generalization of the two-sided assortment optimization model. Specifically, this model consists of two sides (e.g., customers and suppliers) who have preferences over the opposite side in the form of discrete choice models. A matching is realized through a two-step process where the platform’s decision is to initially present to each agent on one side an assortment of users of the opposite side. The ultimate goal of the platform is to maximize the total expected revenue collected from the matching. Because of the computational complexity of this problem, we focus on the design of approximation algorithms with constant-factor guarantees for the constrained version of the problem under general choice preferences. First, to the best of our knowledge, we are the first to draw connections with the literature of submodular optimization and show that one-sided choice-oblivious approaches perform arbitrarily badly. Second, we show that, for the general setting, there exists a two-sided choice-aware randomized algorithm that achieves a [Formula: see text]-approximation factor, which is the best possible. Third, we design an algorithm that is asymptotically optimal when one side follows the well-known multinomial logit (MNL) choice model under the small probability regime. Fourth, we provide a simple and effective algorithm with a [Formula: see text]-approximation guarantee for the unconstrained setting, with both sides following MNL models. Finally, we assess the performance of our proposed methods with a detailed computational study and discuss several extensions. Funding: M. radar.title: Multi-AI agent framework reveals the “oxide gatekeeper” in aluminum nanoparticle oxidation
radar.venue_raw: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
radar.summary: Aluminum nanoparticles (ANPs) are among the most energy-dense solid fuels, yet the atomic mechanisms governing their transition from passivated particles to highly reactive states remain elusive. This stems from a fundamental computational bottleneck: Ab initio methods offer quantum-level fidelity but are restricted to small spatiotemporal scales (<500 atoms, picoseconds), while empirical force fields lack the reactive fidelity required for complex combustion environments. Here, we bridge this gap by employing a human-audited, multiagent framework to make the development and validation of a task-specific machine learning potential (MLP) more traceable and auditable. The workflow coordinates active learning, model evaluation, validation evidence, and human expert review, while leaving scientific interpretation and model-use decisions under researcher control. This collaborative cycle ensures quantum mechanical accuracy while exhibiting near-linear scalability. Strikingly, our simulations reveal a temperature-regulated dual-mode oxidation mechanism: At moderate temperatures, the oxide shell acts as a dynamic “gatekeeper,” regulating oxidation through a “breathing mode” of transient nanochannels; above a critical threshold, a “rupture mode” leads to shell failure and rapid combustion. Importantly, we resolve a decades-old controversy by demonstrating that aluminum cation outward diffusion, rather than oxygen transport, dominates mass transfer in studied regimes, with diffusion coefficients consistently exceeding those of oxygen by 2 to 3 orders of magnitude. These results provide an atomistic framework for interpreting ANP reactivity and illustrate how human-audited agentic workflows can make domain-specific reactive MLP development and deployment more reproducible.
radar.summary_short: Aluminum nanoparticles (ANPs) are among the most energy-dense solid fuels, yet the atomic mechanisms governing their transition from passivated particles to highly reactive states remain elusive.

Preserved higher-order mentalising during strategic interactions after medial prefrontal cortex damage
radar.summary: Abstract Mentalising, the ability to infer the beliefs and intentions of others, is essential for successful social interaction. Previous studies have implicated the medial prefrontal cortex in mentalising, but whether this region is necessary for higher-order mentalising remains unclear. Here we show that people with focal damage to the medial prefrontal cortex retain the ability to engage in higher-order mentalising during a strategic social game. We compare their performance with patients with brain damage in other regions and lesion-free participants. Individuals with medial prefrontal cortex damage achieve similar rewards and use comparable mentalising strategies, but they are slower when making strategic decisions. Computational modelling indicates that this slowing reflects a greater tendency to require evidence before committing to a choice. Voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping identifies medial prefrontal regions linked to altered decision processes rather than mentalising. These findings suggest that the medial prefrontal cortex supports strategic decisions while higher-order mentalising remains intact.

Previous studies have implicated the medial prefrontal cortex in mentalising, but whether this region is necessary for higher-order mentalising remains unclear.

On the Maximization of Long-Run Conditional Value-at-Risk for Markov Decision Processes
radar.summary: Optimizing Risk-Seeking Sequential Decisions via Conditional Value-at-Risk Decision makers may exhibit risk-seeking preferences in finance, energy operations, and stochastic resource management, yet corresponding Markov decision process (MDP) theories remain underdeveloped. In this paper, “On the Maximization of Long-Run CVaR for Markov Decision Processes,” Xia, Yu, and Wu investigate infinite-horizon MDPs maximizing long-run conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) for instantaneous rewards. They prove optimality for stationary randomized policies and show deterministic policies may fail; an optimal policy randomizes over at most two actions. By converting the original problem into a minimax saddle point formulation, the authors develop solvable linear programming and globally convergent gradient descent algorithms. Results are further extended to joint mean-CVaR optimization and validated on real-world microgrid scheduling data. This work fills gaps for risk-seeking MDPs and delivers practical computation tools for tail-oriented sequential decision making.
radar.summary_short: Optimizing Risk-Seeking Sequential Decisions via Conditional Value-at-Risk Decision makers may exhibit risk-seeking preferences in finance, energy operations, and stochastic resource management, yet corresponding Markov decision process (MDP) theories remain underdeveloped.

radar.title: IntNet: A Communication-Driven Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Cooperative Autonomous Driving
radar.summary: Achieving safety in autonomous driving through Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) is a critical yet challenging task due to non-stationarity, partial observability, and the need for effective coordination among agents. Although earlier cooperative MARL methods have aimed to improve coordination by sharing encoded state observations, we find these strategies are insufficient in safety-critical scenarios. To address this gap, we present IntNet, a novel MARL framework that enhances safety by incorporating the transmission of vehicle intent and adaptive communication scheduling into a unified end-to-end learning paradigm, jointly optimising all components for safe coordination. Central to our approach is an observation prediction module that enables agents to forecast subsequent policy outputs, which they can then share across a vehicle-to-vehicle network. Our model-free architecture employs a Graph Attention Network to process incoming messages and a scheduler component to dynamically optimise the communication graph for bandwidth efficiency. We compare IntNet against state-of-the-art communicative MARL methods in complex urban environments with both autonomous and human-operated vehicles, achieving improved coordination, lower collision rates, and reducing communication efforts by up to 60\%. Through extensive experiments, we assess the framework's learning efficiency, scalability, and the balance between information sharing and bandwidth usage for collision-free trajectories.
radar.summary_short: Achieving safety in autonomous driving through Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) is a critical yet challenging task due to non-stationarity, partial observability, and the need for effective coordination among agents.

radar.title: Bargaining and Contract Forms in Distribution Channels: Why Do Slotting Fees Arise and Linear Contracts Persist?
radar.summary: Two empirical patterns emerge in business-to-business settings, particularly in retail distribution channels such as grocery markets. First, linear contracts are widely observed alongside nonlinear contracts with fixed payments, despite the claimed efficiency advantages of the latter. Second, when fixed payments arise, they often flow from suppliers to retailers (slotting fees) rather than the reverse. We develop and analyze a model of multilateral bargaining in which a supplier negotiates separately with competing retailers to explain these patterns. The key mechanism is a trade-off between two distortions: under linear contracts, wholesale prices reflect bargaining power and can be either above or below the channel-profit-maximizing level, whereas under two-part tariffs, wholesale prices are set to maximize bilateral surplus independently of bargaining power but are systematically too low from an overall channel perspective because of rent shifting across relationships. As a result, neither contractual form uniformly dominates; instead, relative performance depends on how bargaining shapes gains from trade across firms. When bargaining leads to slotting fees, two-part tariffs yield higher channel profits than linear contracts, whereas when it would imply payments from retailers to suppliers, linear contracts may perform better. These findings offer a unified explanation for the persistence of linear contracts alongside two-part tariffs, the direction of fixed payments, and the conditions under which each contractual form is likely to arise. This paper was accepted by Miguel Villas-Boas, marketing. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03426 .
radar.summary_short: Two empirical patterns emerge in business-to-business settings, particularly in retail distribution channels such as grocery markets. radar.title: Cyber Defence, Agentic AI, and the Sociotechnical Paradigm: A Survey of AI-Driven Cybersecurity
radar.venue: International Journal of Applied Smart Interdisciplinary Technologies
radar.venue_raw: International Journal of Applied Smart Interdisciplinary Technologies
radar.summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) are reshaping cybersecurity, moving it from signature-based reactive security to agentic, self-evolving, and proactive operations. However, the fast deployment of autonomous agents entails significant security issues, physical-layer attacks in cyber-physical systems, alignment problems, and advanced social engineering risks jeopardizing the stability of the modern sociotechnical infrastructures. This survey paper, which summarizes and analyses the literature, examines the duality of AI in cybersecurity, exploring its implications for strengthening digital defences and increasing the threat landscape for adversaries. We perform a thorough review of 36 cutting-edge research articles, which are organized into six important areas: self-evolving defensive paradigms, LLM-based intelligent agents, reinforcement learning for autonomous decision-making, security of cyber-physical systems, human-machine co-teaming, and agent alignment. Our synthesis shows that multi-agent collaborations greatly shorten incident response times and automate discovery of vulnerabilities but are also highly vulnerable to prompt injection, training data poisoning, and physical-layer spoofing. Moreover, we identify a shift from model patches to model alignment and constitutional safety at runtime as a prerequisite for securing these systems. We believe that resilient digital defence must also be considered a sociotechnical problem, as there must be agents, autonomous systems, that are governed by other agents, aligned and constitutionally bound, and are able to collaborate, rather than operate completely separately, with human operators.
radar.summary_short: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) are reshaping cybersecurity, moving it from signature-based reactive security to agentic, self-evolving, and proactive operations.

radar.title: Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Control of Multiple Unmanned Surface Vehicle in Neutralizing Threat Vessels
radar.venue: Journal of Institute of Control Robotics and Systems
radar.venue_raw: Journal of Institute of Control Robotics and Systems
radar.summary: This study proposes a cooperative capture system in which two allied unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) jointly deploy a capture net to intercept noncooperative vessels in naval environments. To overcome the limitations of traditional rule-based methods subjected to environmental uncertainties, a multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework is developed within a high-fidelity, unity-based simulation environment incorporating the Gerstner wave and wind disturbance models. Each agent utilizes an egocentric polar coordinate observation space; distance values are normalized via a nonlinear rational function to prioritize close-range sensitivity, while angular discontinuities are resolved through trigonometric transformations. The Multi-Agent POsthumous Credit Assignment algorithm is adopted within a Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution architecture, enabling robust strategy learning through posthumous credit assignment even when agents exit the environment. The reward structure is designed hierarchically, combining sparse event rewards for capture success with dense continuous rewards based on formation maintenance, target approach, and heading alignment. Quantitative experimental results demonstrate that the proposed MARL-based approach significantly outperforms the modified Line-of-Sight guidance law, achieving a 65% capture success rate and a three-fold reduction in formation collapse under dynamic sea conditions. This study confirms that the proposed framework effectively enables autonomous USVs to learn complex, coordinated maneuvers for physical maritime interdiction, providing a robust solution for securing maritime security.
radar.summary_short: This study proposes a cooperative capture system in which two allied unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) jointly deploy a capture net to intercept noncooperative vessels in naval environments.

radar.title: EvolveMAS: A Unified Self-Evolution Framework for Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems
radar.summary: Decentralized multi-agent systems (MAS) enable large language model agents to interact without centralized control. Agents need to adapt to other agents at test time and reuse accumulated experience to refine their interaction strategies for future interactions across cooperative, mixed-motive, and adversarial settings. However, existing approaches often develop adaptation mechanisms for particular interaction settings. This raises a central question: how can decentralized MAS support test-time adaptation and reliable experience reuse across interaction settings? We propose EvolveMAS, a unified self-evolution framework that supports experience-driven adaptation within and across episodes. EvolveMAS pairs each main agent with a dedicated MemoryAgent for test-time memory governance, which maintains isolated Structured Memory outside the main agent's reasoning context. EvolveMAS organizes adaptation into two complementary processes: Within-Episode Online Adaptation and Cross-Episode Knowledge Evolution. During Within-Episode Online Adaptation, MemoryAgent updates episodic, semantic, and working memory from interaction evidence to inform subsequent actions. During Cross-Episode Knowledge Evolution, the main agent uses memory and episode outcomes to distill reusable interaction knowledge comprising partner profiles and interaction strategies for subsequent episodes. Across five benchmarks and six evaluation configurations spanning the three interaction settings, EvolveMAS achieves the highest normalized average score of 77.2 among the compared methods. Ablations show that test-time memory governance and cross-episode knowledge reuse both improve performance. Interaction traces further illustrate how updated memory and distilled knowledge guide subsequent interactions. These results support experience-driven adaptation in decentralized MAS without updating model parameters.

radar.title: Community-Oriented Market Design for Nonprofit Resource Exchange
radar.summary: Unlocking Value Through Nonprofit Resource Sharing Nonprofit organizations often operate under tight budgets while idle equipment, unused space, and shareable skills and expertise are frequently underutilized, with existing resource exchanges in the nonprofit sector limited to bilateral barter or relatively homogeneous resources. In “Community-Oriented Market Design for Nonprofit Resource Exchange,” Huang et al. propose Sharing With a Purpose (SWAP), a resource-sharing system that enables nonprofits to exchange heterogeneous resources without monetary payments. SWAP combines an auction-based process, SWAPcredit valuation, and integer optimization to facilitate multilateral exchanges, allowing nonprofits to obtain needed resources by contributing resources of their own. The authors implement this market design through the SWAP Hub, a digital platform deployed with nonprofit communities in multiple regions. Through repeated exchange episodes, participating organizations have shared not only physical assets but also a wide range of skills, services, and expertise, including marketing, management, event planning, and organizational development. The study demonstrates how innovative market design can unlock latent value in community resources, alleviate resource constraints, and encourage new connections and collaboration among nonprofit organizations.

radar.title: A Survey of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning from the Perspective of Task Characteristics
radar.summary: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), the relationship between agents' rewards determines part of the learning problem. Shared rewards give rise to credit assignment and coordinated action selection; opposed rewards require responses to an adapting opponent. Both relationships occur in mixed tasks. This survey takes these task differences as the starting point for reviewing MARL, complementing classifications based on algorithms, training frameworks, or application domains. The analysis follows task characteristics, interaction types, and algorithmic mechanisms across cooperative, competitive, and mixed cooperative-competitive settings. It covers the basic formulations and training and execution paradigms, then compares representative methods in terms of their mechanisms, applicability, and limitations. Path planning, task allocation, pursuit-evasion and adversarial engagement, autonomous driving, and resource allocation illustrate how information access and operational constraints affect method selection. The concluding discussion concerns non-stationarity, scaling, safety, and the evidence needed for deployment. The comparisons support method selection under stated task conditions, without treating applicability as independent of the task being addressed.
radar.summary_short: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), the relationship between agents' rewards determines part of the learning problem. Shared rewards give rise to credit assignment and coordinated action selection; opposed rewards require responses to an adapting opponent.

radar.title: Multi-agent reinforcement learning for coordinated reservoir releases under conflicting hydropower and irrigation mandates: a climate-analytics evaluation of Pareto-regret and downstream equity
radar.venue_raw: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
radar.summary: Reservoir operators in transboundary basins face a structural conflict: hydropower revenue is maximised by releasing water when electricity prices peak, while irrigation mandates require deliveries timed to crop water demand. Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) has been proposed as a coordination mechanism for such settings, but its evaluation has relied on aggregate reward, which conceals the distribution of regret across agents and the equity consequences for downstream users. The framework defines Pareto-regret as the vector of per-agent deviations from the Pareto frontier of feasible release schedules, and downstream equity as the dispersion of delivered irrigation volume across downstream users. A climate-analytics layer conditions the evaluation on observed hydroclimatic variability. The framework is illustrated with NASA POWER monthly reanalysis air temperature for Harare, Zimbabwe (-17.83, 31.05) over 2000-2023 (312 monthly observations), which shows a mean of 18.914 C and a warming trend of 0.2001 C per decade. The paper derives conditions under which MARL coordination reduces aggregate regret while widening downstream equity gaps, and specifies the evaluation protocol that would detect this trade-off. The contribution is a diagnostic framework, not an empirical demonstration of MARL performance.
radar.summary_short: Reservoir operators in transboundary basins face a structural conflict: hydropower revenue is maximised by releasing water when electricity prices peak, while irrigation mandates require deliveries timed to crop water demand.

radar.title: Strategic Calibration in LLM Multi-Agent Systems: Audited Pivot Scoring for Truthful Elicitation
radar.summary: In large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems, reported confidence increasingly determines the allocation of scarce downstream attention, computation, and decision influence. This makes reporting strategic: an agent may overstate the relevance of its contribution even when its underlying belief is well calibrated. Existing calibration methods largely assume passive reporting and therefore do not address strategic incentives created when confidence determines downstream allocation. We formulate strategic calibration as a reporting-layer incentive problem and propose the Audited Pivot Scoring Mechanism (APSM). APSM offsets platform-controlled allocation benefits, uses inverse-propensity-weighted sparse audits, charges the Clarke pivot externality, and applies a strictly proper score. Under the stated model assumptions, truthful reporting is the unique expected-utility best response. We also characterize approximate execution and the audit-variance trade-off. Calculator-free experiments show that LLM agents inflate confidence under Top-$K$ incentives. With a shared agent-local utility interface, LLM agents reduce distortion under both Compensated Proper Scoring (CPS) and APSM. CPS achieves higher exact allocation match, whereas APSM yields lower Brier loss and numerically fewer cutoff crossings. Experiments further show that APSM enlarges the utility margin against allocation-changing deviations by $1.93\times$ and improves robustness under approximate execution. These results support incentive-aware elicitation as a distinct layer for reliable multi-agent coordination.
radar.summary_short: In large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems, reported confidence increasingly determines the allocation of scarce downstream attention, computation, and decision influence.

radar.title: Single and multi-winner auctions with performance obligation
radar.summary: Auctioning access rights to private providers through competitive tendering has become a central instrument for governments to regulate markets and public services. While efficient in allocating licenses, such auctions may generate monopolistic market structures with adverse effects on consumer welfare. We experimentally evaluate two policy interventions to mitigate these outcomes: introducing post-tender competition and imposing minimum production obligations on winning firms. Our results show that performance obligations substantially improve welfare by raising output and consumer surplus, albeit at the cost of reduced auction revenue. Extending the design with additional treatments, we demonstrate that genuine competition yields even stronger welfare gains. These findings highlight a trade-off between government revenue and consumer welfare in auction design. We conclude that while obligations are an effective tool to counter monopoly distortions, sustaining competition remains essential to maximise total surplus at the market level.

radar.title: AI Digital Twin for Cloud Cyber Security
radar.venue: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
radar.venue_raw: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
radar.summary: The key advantage of cloud computing is scalability and flexibility of infrastructure, however, the growing complexity of cloud environments has led to numerous security issues. Current security systems are largely reactive, which means that any detected attacks have already taken place. This paper suggests the use of the AI-based Digital Twin technology for cybersecurity in cloud environments, providing the possibility of creating a virtual copy of the cloud environment that can be used for continuous monitoring, attack simulation, and security testing. The proposed framework uses AI/ML algorithms for anomaly detection, attacks' classification, and risk assessment in conjunction with Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) in order to achieve collaboration and adaptability of security response. The system includes cloud resource monitoring, attacks simulation, security logging, alert generation, access control by roles, and security analysis dashboard. The development of the system takes place using MERN stack architecture with Digital Twin synchronization of virtual cloud resources and their metrics. With the combination of Digital Twin technology, AI-based threat detection and multi-agent decision making, the proposed framework can provide enhanced proactivity,adaptiveness, and real-time performance of cybersecurity in cloud environments.

Current security systems are largely reactive, which means that any detected attacks have already taken place.

radar.title: A Factor-6 Truthful-in-Expectation Mechanism for Cascade Position Auctions
radar.summary: Position auctions require assigning advertisers to positions and determining their display order. Under cascade behavior, earlier clicks prevent users from reaching later placements, coupling the click probabilities of selected advertisements. Existing methods achieve constant-factor welfare approximation and monotone logarithmic-factor approximation separately, leaving open whether both guarantees can be attained simultaneously. The difficulty is that welfare-preserving rounding need not maintain the monotonicity of individual click-through rates required for truthful bidding. We resolve this problem by developing a polynomial-time randomized mechanism that achieves a factor-6 welfare approximation and truthfulness in expectation for arbitrary public advertiser-position click probabilities. The mechanism optimizes a reach-weighted linear relaxation and converts its solution into feasible ordered allocations through matching decomposition, probability-bounded grouping, and calibrated attenuation. This construction compensates for cascade dependence and ensures that each advertiser's expected click-through rate equals exactly one sixth of its fractional click coordinate. The resulting identity transfers the monotonicity of the fractional allocation to the implemented mechanism, enabling exact incentive-compatible payments while preserving the welfare guarantee. The allocation lottery and payments are computable in polynomial bit time, with exact sampling in expected polynomial time.
radar.summary_short: Position auctions require assigning advertisers to positions and determining their display order. Under cascade behavior, earlier clicks prevent users from reaching later placements, coupling the click probabilities of selected advertisements.

radar.title: Toward unified intelligence in renewable-dominant power systems: a survey of hybrid forecasting, explainable AI, and multi-agent optimization
radar.summary: The transition toward renewable-dominant power systems has introduced significant operational challenges due to increased uncertainty, reduced system inertia, and the proliferation of distributed energy resources. While artificial intelligence (AI) techniques have been widely adopted for renewable energy forecasting and grid optimization, existing studies primarily address these components in isolation, leading to fragmented system-level intelligence. This paper presents a comprehensive survey that systematically integrates three critical dimensions of modern intelligent energy systems: hybrid forecasting, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), and multi-agent optimization. First, we review advanced hybrid learning architectures, including decomposition-based models, ensemble frameworks, and deep learning-metaheuristic hybrids, highlighting their effectiveness in capturing nonlinear and stochastic renewable dynamics. Second, we examine XAI techniques that enhance transparency, interpretability, and trust in AI-driven energy systems. Third, we analyze the evolution from centralized optimization to distributed collective intelligence using multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), swarm intelligence, and federated learning paradigms. Unlike conventional surveys, this work provides a unified system-level perspective by explicitly linking predictive uncertainty with decentralized decision-making and explainability mechanisms. A conceptual integration framework is presented to demonstrate how probabilistic forecasting, risk-aware MARL policies, and interpretable models can jointly enable robust and scalable grid operation. Furthermore, we identify key research challenges related to scalability, computational efficiency, uncertainty propagation, and real-time deployment. This survey offers a structured reference for researchers and practitioners and outlines future directions toward trustworthy, adaptive, and cooperative AI-driven energy systems.
radar.summary_short: The transition toward renewable-dominant power systems has introduced significant operational challenges due to increased uncertainty, reduced system inertia, and the proliferation of distributed energy resources.

radar.title: Autonomous biomedical research with an artificial intelligence agent
radar.summary: Biomedical research is increasingly constrained by repetitive, fragmented workflows that slow discovery. We introduce Biomni, a general-purpose biomedical artificial intelligence agent that autonomously executes diverse research tasks. To map the biomedical action space, Biomni’s action-discovery agent mines tools, databases, and protocols from thousands of publications across 25 domains, building a unified agentic environment. Its general-purpose architecture integrates large language model reasoning with retrieval-augmented planning and code-based execution, dynamically composing workflows without predefined templates. Systematic benchmarking shows strong generalization across heterogeneous tasks—causal gene prioritization, drug repurposing, rare-disease diagnosis, microbiome analysis, and molecular cloning—without task-specific tuning. Real-world case studies demonstrate Biomni interpreting multimodal datasets, optimizing protein stability, orchestrating wet-lab instruments, and generating experimentally testable protocols. Biomni envisions artificial intelligence augmenting human scientists and accelerating discovery.

radar.title: Implementation via political parties
radar.summary: We address the implementation of public policies (alternatives) when the feasible set is unknown to the planner. The implementing agents are the political parties, who know the feasible set. They care about the implemented alternative, which reflects their ideology, and their share in parliament and office. They face a mechanism that, given the alternatives proposed by all parties, asks the voters to rank them and determines the chosen alternative and the shares in parliament and office. We identify conditions on parties’ preferences that guarantee the socially optimal policy is the outcome of the unique pure strategy Nash equilibrium of the electoral game played by the parties. The existence of the equilibrium does not require any assumptions about the parties’ ideology. To ensure uniqueness, shares must prevail over ideology: office or parliamentary shares in two-party systems, and strictly office shares in systems with more than two parties.

radar.title: A Deep Learning Framework for Evaluating and Mitigating Prompt Injection in LLM Agents
radar.summary: In the world of large language models (LLMs), prompt injection attacks are a severe security risk that can circumvent the instructions given to AI agents and potentially cause damage. In agentic architectures, the vulnerabilities are magnified because of the increased attack surfaces which are present in the use of tools, APIs and chains of reasoning. The vulnerabilities are compounded in agentic architectures as the tools used, APIs called, and chains of reasoning become a larger attack surface, resulting in an increased sense of unreliability. Paraphrased, adaptive, and context-aware attacks are not thwarted by rule-based and static prompt engineering defenses. This paper introduces a deep learning-based approach to detecting and thwarting prompt injection attacks in LLM agent systems. Uses a hybrid model of known and customer-generated adversarial prompts to combine transformer-based classification, semantic risk-scoring and adaptive mitigation procedures. Stratified data splits are used in the experiments, as are synthetic attack generation and rule-based, BERT and zero-shot LLM classifiers. In terms of precision, recall, F1 score and AUC, the proposed framework is found to be better than all the baselines. Attack of instruction override, data extraction and tool misuse are greatly enhanced and resistant to adversarial scenarios that are not seen and adaptable. The mitigation module achieves high task utility; low false positive rates and the high success rate of the attacks is significantly reduced. Overall, the framework demonstrates that it is possible to integrate detection, risk estimation, and mitigation in a single pipeline, resulting in a great improvement in the security of LLM agents, while not burdening them with significant computing costs. It further highlights the importance of security layers before deploying LLM agents to the real world as the input they receive can be adversarial and continuously change, requiring a mixture of machine learning and structured control to ensure they remain safe and reliable across different application areas. Scalable AI systems deployment safety improvements involve multi-agent security, real-time learning, and multimodal prompt injection detection in the future.

radar.title: Online LLM Inference Routing for Multi-Agent Systems under Long-Term Budget and Layered Privacy Constraints
radar.summary: Abstract The Cloud-Edge-End (CEE) collaborative architecture has become a key paradigm for deploying highly intelligent multi-agent systems with low latency and high energy efficiency. Existing studies on efficient task offloading in CEE, however, either overlook long-term financial budget constraints from commercial API token usage and edge computing leasing, or inadequately handle layered information-sharing and privacy restrictions in decentralized autonomous agents. This paper investigates online inference routing to minimize the computational and communication overhead of large language model (LLM) workloads under long-term budget constraints, agent intent-sharing limitations, and un-known future prompt lengths. We propose a budget-aware online optimization framework that uses Lyapunov optimization to decouple long-term financial constraints, and show that the decoupled problem forms a generalized ordinal potential game. To address heterogeneous information-sharing restrictions, we design an adaptive best response algorithm for cooperative environments with shared decision information, and a multi-agent distributed routing algorithm for limited-information environments, enabling efficient offloading without inter-agent intent sharing. Theoretical analysis provides conditional performance and queue-length bounds and establishes finite convergence of the per-slot solvers. Simulations on distributed inference testbeds show that our scheme reduces the inference overhead of heterogeneous agentic tasks while achieving a favorable trade-off between performance and actual token expenditure.

radar.title: BE-CTDE: Blockchain-Enabled Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Anomaly Detection and Token Economics
radar.summary: Multi-agent reinforcement learning supports cooperative decision-making in Internet of Things systems, but strategic deviations can disrupt coordination and undermine confidence in the training process. This paper proposes Blockchain-Enabled Centralized Training and Decentralized Execution (BE-CTDE), which uses blockchain as an active training-management layer. A behavioral verifier compares executed trajectories with shared-policy recommendations; its flags drive a token mechanism combining slashing, burning, rewards, and compensation. Retained balances determine each agent's contribution to the global policy update, connecting auditable behavior to learning influence. We derive a one-round incentive condition that accounts for action-dependent compensation and the payoff from deviation, and a finite expected exclusion-time bound under explicit conditional detection and accounting assumptions, showing perfect detection is unnecessary. An exact finite-population capacity bound characterizes the limits of the population-relative detector. In multi-agent path finding experiments, BE-CTDE outperforms a state-of-the-art learning-based path planner with substantially higher success rates under attack, even when adversaries form the majority. It also outperforms partially defended baselines in all configurations, with collision rates up to 35% lower than under detection without economic consequences and up to 43% lower than under conventional stake slashing. Together, these results characterize how behavioral verification and token feedback can support accountable cooperative learning.
radar.summary_short: Multi-agent reinforcement learning supports cooperative decision-making in Internet of Things systems, but strategic deviations can disrupt coordination and undermine confidence in the training process.

radar.title: Preference-Guided Cooperation in Multi-Objective Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
radar.summary: Multi-objective multi-agent reinforcement learning (MOMARL) addresses agent coordination and objective trade-offs simultaneously while optimising overall system performance. Existing work tends to treat multi-agent cooperation and multi-objective optimisation as largely independent components of a learning problem, which amounts to an exorbitant complexity except in trivial cases. We study here whether the structure provided by multiple objectives can itself be exploited to facilitate cooperation, rather than being treated as an additional optimisation challenge. We formulate MOMARL at both the team and individual levels and introduce objective-wise counterfactual credit assignment to evaluate each agent's contribution across the team objectives. We propose Meta-Gradient Informed Multi-Objective Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MIRL), with static (MIRL-S) and dynamic (MIRL-D) variants. By incorporating meta-gradient information, MIRL enables agents to learn how to prioritise objectives individually while collectively optimising the system-level objective, allowing the multi-objective structure to directly guide cooperation. Experiments on a multi-objective multiple particle environment show that our methods improve Pareto-front quality over baselines, with the dynamic variant achieving the strongest performance.

radar.title: Belief-Conditioned Multi-Agent Actor Critic for Decentralized LLM Collaboration
radar.summary: Recent work has explored optimizing LLM collaboration through Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), but many approaches still rely on predefined workflows, limiting efficiency and scalability. Decentralized LLM collaboration is challenging because agents execute independently with limited communication, share a joint objective, and must infer useful information from communication traces. In this paper, we propose BCMAAC, a Belief-Conditioned Multi-Agent Actor-Critic method that maintains beliefs over contextual information and uses them to facilitate training. Experiments on Minecraft game-playing, web searching and tool-using tasks show that BCMAAC improves task performance and collaborative behavior compared to naive actor-critic baselines. The improvements are particularly pronounced in multi-turn tasks with richer contextual information, where belief modeling provides a clear advantage.

radar.title: Context-Aware Cooperative Gating for Knowledge-Controlled Value Factorization in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
radar.venue: International Journal of Software Engineering and Knowledge Engineering
radar.venue_raw: International Journal of Software Engineering and Knowledge Engineering
radar.summary: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning under partial observability requires decentralized agents to act from incomplete local information. Value-decomposition methods such as VDN and QMIX do not control when teammate-related knowledge may influence an agent’s local utility, and an uncontrolled teammate-conditioned term can distort decisions at timesteps where no ally is observable. We propose CA-QMIX, a context-aware value factorization method that uses ally visibility as a knowledge signal for decentralized agent control. Each agent combines an individual decision branch with an attention-based cooperative knowledge branch through a visibility-conditioned gate that scales the cooperative contribution and is hard-masked to zero when no ally is observable. The gated utilities are combined by a QMIX-style monotonic mixer, which we prove preserves Individual-Global-Max consistency, and a mixer-level Δ-Q regularizer discourages cooperative corrections that lower the greedy value of the base branch. Experiments on seven SMAC v1 and SMAC v2 scenarios against six value-decomposition baselines show that CA-QMIX attains the highest mean final win rate and the best mean rank over the seven scenarios and improves on QMIX in all three randomized SMAC v2 scenarios. Ablations show that most of the gain comes from the cooperative branch, that its visibility conditioning helps when correctly aligned (misaligned visibility degrades performance under randomized placement), and that the form of the gate is not critical: a binary gate suffices and the hard no-ally mask has no measurable cost.

radar.title: A Truthful-in-Expectation 2-Approximation for Pair-Specific Cascade Auctions in AI-Generated Content
radar.summary: Generative AI interfaces can insert sponsored content at multiple points in an answer, where click-through rates (CTRs) depend on the advertiser-position pair. Under the cascade model, users read ads sequentially and stop after their first click, so both ad assignment and display order affect welfare. For arbitrary pair-specific CTRs, Balseiro et al. (WWW 2026) gave a $4/(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation whose monotonicity has not been established, and a monotone $O(\log m)$-approximation for $m$ candidate positions. Earlier truthful constant-factor mechanisms require factorized CTR models and do not apply. Whether monotonicity is compatible with a constant-factor approximation in this general setting was left open by that work. We give a polynomial-time mechanism for arbitrary pair-specific CTRs and any limit on displayed ads that is truthful and individually rational in expectation and achieves a 2-approximation to optimal cascade welfare. Our mechanism selects an advertiser-position matching and a designated last ad, then randomly thins earlier ads so that each selected ad's expected cascade CTR is the same fraction of its standalone CTR. This yields an exact closed-form expression for expected welfare, which we maximize over a bid-independent lottery range using linear programming. Exact optimization ensures monotonicity, while a random-prefix decomposition proves the factor-two guarantee, which is tight for this range. We also show that exactly optimizing the previous welfare surrogate can violate monotonicity, and evaluate welfare and running time on synthetic instances.

radar.title: Collective Emergent Alignment: Measuring and Amplifying Interaction-Induced Reasoning Alignment in Multi-Agent LLMs
radar.summary: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems can exhibit emergent behaviors through interaction, yet whether a similar phenomenon exists for reasoning alignment remains largely unexplored. We study whether agent interaction produces additional reference-grounded reasoning alignment beyond matched individual self-refinement, and introduce REMAP (Reference-Entailment-Matrix for Agentic Process), a framework that quantifies this effect through Semantic Coverage and interaction-specific alignment gains. Across diverse model families and two multi-hop reasoning benchmarks, we observe broadly positive interaction gains, particularly on reasoning content that depends on integrating evidence distributed across agents. These gains are consistently associated with independently measured peer-information recovery, while further analysis reveals composition-dependent heterogeneity effects and asymmetric information transfer across agent capability levels. Motivated by these findings, we further introduce a fact-level multi-agent communication framework that replaces full reasoning-trace exchange with compact, gap-aware, and selectively routed information. Our experiments show that compact fact exchange improves reasoning alignment and task performance while reducing communication overhead, whereas more selective communication exposes a trade-off between acquiring distributed information, retaining local content, and communication efficiency. Overall, our results show that collective emergent alignment can be quantified, linked to information-transfer patterns, and used to guide more effective multi-agent communication.

radar.title: Centralized Critics for N-Agent Ad Hoc Teamwork
radar.summary: Centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) has become the dominant paradigm in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), motivating extensive study of what privileged information should be made available to the critic during training. While prior work has examined the role of global state in fully cooperative settings, the design of centralized critics for N-agent ad hoc teamwork - in which dynamically varying set of learning agents must coordinate with an arbitrary set of uncontrolled teammates drawn from an unknown distribution - remains poorly understood. We study this question by comparing two natural classes of advantage estimators: controlled history estimators, which condition only on the observation and action histories of the learner's own agents, and joint history estimators, which additionally condition on the histories of the uncontrolled teammates. We prove that both estimators are unbiased and characterize the conditions under which the joint history estimate attains strictly lower variance than its controlled counterpart. Empirically, joint history critics match or outperform controlled history critics across a range of NAHT tasks, yielding improved sample efficiency and final returns. Together, these results provide both a theoretical justification and an empirical recommendation for incorporating uncontrolled agent histories into centralized critics for N-agent ad hoc teamwork.

In Which Matching Markets Do Costly Compatibility Inspections Lead to a Deadlock?
radar.summary: When Learning About a Match Stalls the Market In many matching markets, participants must investigate whether a match is feasible. When inspection is costly, participants may delay investigating a potential match until both sides have effectively committed. Such caution can cause each side to wait for others to act, creating an “information deadlock.” In their article, “In Which Matching Markets Do Costly Compatibility Inspections Lead to a Deadlock?” Immorlica, Kanoria, and Lu study this problem in random two-sided markets. They characterize how deadlock depends on the market balance, market connectivity, and the chance that inspections succeed. Using statistical physics tools, their analysis identifies phase transitions between deadlock-free and deadlocked markets. The findings offer design guidance: More choice is not always better; match rates are highest at the deadlock phase boundary; and parallel inspections and clearer participant differentiation can reduce the extent to which waiting chains stall the market.

radar.title: Trading Off Business and Family Investments: Evidence from U.S. Entrepreneurial Households
radar.summary: Investing in children’s human capital reduces business investments for U.S. entrepreneurial households. Using financial account data of 90,000 small businesses linked to their owners and a regression discontinuity design that compares the business performance of households with college-aged dependents (18–22) to those with near-college-aged dependents (14–17), I show that business revenues and expenses decline sharply when owners’ children reach age 18. Despite the declines, profitability and productivity remain largely unaffected, suggesting a general downsizing rather than a loss in efficiency. Heterogeneity analysis shows that downsizing is concentrated among highly indebted owner households and businesses with volatile cash flows. For each dollar increase in household spending associated with a child turning 18, business expenses decline by $2.26. These findings are consistent with entrepreneurial parents reallocating capital from business investments toward their children’s human capital, as both compete for the same pool of internal family financial resources. radar.title: Multi-agent reinforcement learning for reservoir cascade release scheduling: a climate-analytics evaluation of downstream low-flow equity under forecast uncertainty
radar.venue_raw: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
radar.summary: Cascade reservoir operators must release water under uncertain inflow forecasts while satisfying competing demands for hydropower, irrigation and downstream environmental flows. The framework is formalised as a constrained Markov game with a lexicographic objective: maximise energy revenue subject to a probabilistic low-flow equity constraint at downstream reaches. A decomposed soft actor-critic architecture with a centralised equity critic is proposed, and a formal analysis establishes conditions under which the learned joint policy satisfies the equity constraint with high probability. The framework is evaluated conceptually against rule-based and single-agent benchmarks using a stylised three-reservoir cascade, with forecast uncertainty represented by ensemble inflow scenarios. The analysis identifies a structural trade-off between revenue and equity that widens as forecast uncertainty increases, and shows that equity-aware credit assignment reduces the frequency of severe low-flow violations relative to revenue-only learning. The contribution is a formalisation and algorithmic design for equity-aware MARL in cascade scheduling, together with a set of testable propositions about the conditions under which decentralised learning can deliver equitable low-flow outcomes.

radar.title: Local Algebraic Stability of Wasserstein Gradient Descent-Ascent and Mean Field Langevin Dynamics without Spectral Gap
radar.summary: We study the local stability of Wasserstein gradient descent-ascent (GDA) for entropy regularized two-player zero-sum games on noncompact domains. When one or both equilibrium measures fail to satisfy a Poincaré inequality, the spectral gap arguments underlying local exponential convergence are unavailable. we show that Wasserstein GDA converges algebraically to the mixed Nash equilibrium in chi-squared divergence, provided the initial relative density is a small perturbation in $L^2$ with bounded algebraic moments. The proof has two main ingredients: a cancellation in a negative Sobolev energy estimate, and a bootstrap argument that keeps the moments bounded uniformly in time. For polynomial-tailed equilibria, we construct perturbations supported far out in the tails that survive over diffusive time scales, which gives algebraic lower bounds on the worst-case relaxation rate. We also establish analogous local algebraic stability and lower bound results for mean-field Langevin dynamics, when the equilibrium fails to satisfy a spectral gap.

radar.title: Autonomous AI-Driven Security Operations Centers (Autonomous SOC): Agentic Orchestration, Real-Time Incident Response, and Multi-Agent Defensive Playbooks
radar.venue_raw: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
radar.summary: Abstract—Contemporary enterprise Security Operations Centers (SOCs) are on the brink of systemic collapse driven by three converging factors: exponential alert fatigue (>25,000 uninvestigated alerts daily per enterprise), acute global cybersecurity workforce shortages, and the emergence of automated, machine-speed cyber threats executing multi-stage Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) in sub-minute time horizons. Traditional Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) platforms rely on brittle, rigid, hard-coded linear playbooks that fail when adversaries deviate slightly from known MITRE ATT&CK patterns. The paradigm of the Autonomous AI-Driven SOC (Autonomous SOC) establishes a transformative architecture that replaces rigid rule engines with specialized collaborative Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) powered by fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). In an Autonomous SOC, decentralized cognitive agents autonomously triage alerts, execute deep forensic graph correlation, synthesize non-linear incident playbooks, isolate compromised endpoints via zero-trust API invocations, and conduct automated counter-adversarial negotiations. However, deploying autonomous agentic execution in mission-critical defensive infrastructure exposes severe risks: catastrophic hallucination loops during remediation, prompt injection propagation across defensive pipelines, decision deadlock, and unauthorized disruption of legitimate enterprise operations. This paper presents an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of Autonomous SOC architectures. We formalize incident response as a decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) under dynamic threat uncertainty, model consensus verification over cryptographic remediation DAGs, and establish a dual-tier human-on-the-loop (HOTL) safety gating mechanism. Furthermore, we construct an enterprise SOC evaluation testbed spanning 10,000 multi-stage attack scenarios across real-world enterprise topologies. Our empirical findings demonstrate that our multi-agent autonomous framework slashes Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) from 18.4 minutes to 4.2 seconds and Mean Time to Remediate (MTTR) from 42.6 minutes to 18.2 seconds (a 99.3% reduction) while preserving a 99.6% remediation accuracy against MITRE ATT&CK kill chains. Finally, we formulate open challenges in adversarial prompt-injection resilience, continuous defensive co-evolution, and liability attribution under international cyber law.

radar.title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Computer Agriculture Shared-Irrigation Scheduling Under Groundwater Rights Uncertainty: A Nash-Regret Evaluation
radar.venue_raw: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
radar.summary: Shared irrigation schemes allocate a common aquifer among competing plots whose groundwater rights are incompletely specified, so that each irrigator's feasible extraction depends on others' choices and on a legal entitlement that may be revised. the present analysis formalises shared-irrigation scheduling as a stochastic game in which agents hold private beliefs over their rights and evaluates multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) against a Nash-regret criterion rather than against average reward. Because no field deployment is available, the study is a design-and-operating-characteristics analysis: a before-after-control-impact (BACI) evaluation design is characterised under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5 and intraclass correlation = 0.64, using 2000 replications per design cell across cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The analysis derives a regret decomposition that separates entitlement uncertainty from strategic uncertainty, states conditions under which independent learners converge to a Nash equilibrium of the induced scheduling game, and reports the power and minimum detectable effect of the BACI design that would be used to evaluate such a scheduler. The contribution is a formal bridge between MARL convergence guarantees and the inferential limits of the agricultural evaluation designs that would test them.

radar.title: Constant Regret Primal-Dual Policy for Multiway Dynamic Matching
radar.summary: We study a discrete-time dynamic multiway matching model. There are finitely many agent types that arrive stochastically and wait to be matched. State-of-the-art dynamic matching policies in the literature require the knowledge of all system parameters to determine an optimal basis of the fluid relaxation, and focus on controlling the number of waiting agents using only matches within the optimal basis. In this paper, we propose a primal-dual policy that schedules matches for future arrivals based on an estimator for the dual solution. Our policy does not require the knowledge of the arrival rates and operates with greater flexibility as it does not restrict matches to only the match types within an optimal basis. We show that our policy is the first to achieve constant regret at all times under unknown arrival rates, and when the arrival rates are known, it achieves the optimal scaling. Furthermore, when the arrival rates are known, the primal-dual policy significantly outperforms alternative dynamic matching policies in several numerical simulations. radar.summary: This book develops a unified governance framework for systems that retrieve, generate, infer, remember and act on information from large language models and retrieval augmented pipelines to autonomous multi agent systems. Eleven chapters and eight appendices integrate three disciplinary lenses-technology, law and economics-across the full lifecycle: data quality, lineage and provenance; global data protection law and intellectual property; the economics of data governance; digital trust, cybersecurity and zero-trust architecture; ethics and responsible AI; governing generative AI pipelines; governing agentic AI and multi-agent systems; data governance in elections and the public sphere; AI regulation across six jurisdictions; and the design of a governance control plane for 2030. radar.title: HA-DiPO: Diffusion Policy Optimization for Heterogeneous Cooperative Transport
radar.summary: Cooperative transport with heterogeneous legged robots requires coordinating different motion capabilities while supporting an unfixed shared payload. We present HA-DiPO (Heterogeneous-Agent Diffusion Policy Optimization), a hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework under centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE). The framework decouples team-level coordination from embodiment-specific motion control: at the high level, a centralized critic uses team-value estimates to jointly train independent coordination policies, aligning robot-specific action responses with a shared transport objective; at the low level, embodiment-specific robust motion policies track the coordination commands. The high-level diffusion policies offer more flexible action distributions than single-Gaussian parameterizations, allowing potentially multimodal coordination responses to be represented. The coordination policies learn from scratch through reward-driven simulator interaction without demonstrations. At execution, each robot generates coordination commands using only local robot and payload observations, without partner-state inputs or inter-robot messages. Simulation comparisons show that HA-DiPO achieves higher final mean returns and velocity-tracking success rates, as well as lower velocity errors, than the evaluated baselines. Real-world experiments further demonstrate quadrupedal-wheeled-legged and human-robot cooperative transport.

radar.title: Dynamic Contract Design with Learning
radar.summary: Incentivizing Effort While Learning the Market Condition When a firm hires an agent to generate customers in a new market, neither party initially knows whether the market is favorable. In “Dynamic Contract Design with Learning,” Wang, Liang, and Sun study the interaction between learning and moral hazard: effort is costly and unobservable, so a missing arrival may reflect an unfavorable market, bad luck, or shirking. The firm’s goal is to design a dynamic contract governing arrival-based payments and termination, thereby motivating effort while learning whether to continue. Yet shirking can make the principal more pessimistic than the agent and create scope to manipulate future payments. The authors prove that an optimal contract inducing full effort until termination exists, but computing it appears prohibitively complex. They develop two simple online contracts with payments and termination thresholds fixed in advance. Both induce full effort and achieve O(ln T) regret over T periods against a first-best, full-information benchmark. A matching Ω(ln T) lower bound proves rate optimality. The results extend to continuous time and differing prior beliefs.

radar.title: On the Nash equilibrium for a model of traffic flow
radar.summary: The paper consider a conservation law model of traffic flow on a highway, where each driver chooses an optimal departure time $τ^d$, based on a departure cost $\varphi(τ^d)$ and an arrival cost $ψ(τ^a)$. Nash equilibria are studied, where no driver can reduce his own cost by changing his departure time. The first results provide continuity estimates on the arrival time, depending on the distribution of departures. In terms of the ${\bf L}^1$ distance, we show that the corresponding map is Hölder continuous with exponent $1/2$ in Lagrangian variables (labelling individual drivers), and Lipschitz continuous in Eulerian space variables. Concerning the regularity of the a Nash equilibrium, our results show that, when the total number of drivers is sufficiently large, a queue alway forms at the entrance of the highway and the corresponding traffic density contains a shock. Moreover, for any number of drivers (possibly small), we prove that for generic $\mathcal C^2$ cost functions $\varphi, ψ$ the Nash equilibrium solution still contains a shock. In the last section of the paper, assuming that the initial departure rate is not a Nash equilibrium, we consider an evolution equation for the departure rate, where each driver keeps changing his daily departure time in order to reduce his own cost. It is proved that this nonlocal integro-differential evolution equation admits a unique solution, globally in time. This provides some theoretical support to earlier numerical simulations, which indicated the dynamic instability of the Nash equilibrium and the possible existence of a chaotic attractor.

Who Directs the Control Tower? Customer vs. Supplier-Managed Inventory in Supply Chains
radar.summary: Information distortion and incentive misalignment often undermine supply chain performance. In response, many firms adopt a “control tower” approach, whereby one party assumes responsibility for replenishment decisions across the supply chain. Industry examples showed that this role may be assigned to the customer, Customer-Managed Inventory (CMI), or to the supplier, Supplier-Managed Inventory (SMI). This paper investigates when one governance structure is preferable. We study a two-echelon, one-to-many supply chain consisting of a single supplier and a customer operating multiple warehouses. We characterize optimal base-stock policies and equilibrium holding-cost-sharing parameters under CMI and SMI and benchmark them against decentralized operations and a fully centralized system. Two primary forces shape the choice between CMI and SMI: the relative shortage penalty costs of the two parties and the structure of the customer’s distribution network. Specifically, CMI is preferred when the customer faces relatively higher shortage penalties and operates in a more asymmetric environment—for example, when demand is concentrated in a subset of its warehouses or when replenishment lead times vary substantially across these locations. In contrast, SMI is favored under opposite conditions. We further examine how intertemporal and interspatial demand correlations affect this comparison. A key finding is that, although neither CMI nor SMI achieves the first-best outcome, their efficiency loss relative to full centralization is typically small. Calibrated numerical studies based on four industry cases disentangle the incremental value of information sharing, decision-right transfer, and cost sharing, showing that most performance gains stem from decision-right transfer supported by appropriate holding-cost sharing. This paper was accepted by Jayashankar Swaminathan, operations management. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.02137 .

Globally guided multi-agent reinforcement learning with decoupled critics for cooperative UAV path planning
radar.summary: Abstract Cooperative path planning for multiple unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) requires the simultaneous achievement of target navigation, collision avoidance, and formation coordination in complex obstacle environments. Existing multi-agent reinforcement learning methods often suffer from sparse rewards, local deadlocks, and conflicts between formation maintenance and obstacle avoidance, which can destabilize policy learning. To address these issues, this paper proposes a Globally Guided Decoupled-Critic Multi-Agent Soft Actor-Critic algorithm (GDC-MASAC). RRT $$^*$$ -based global guidance provides reference waypoints for the leader UAV, reducing inefficient exploration and local deadlocks. Three decoupled Critic branches separately evaluate target navigation, formation maintenance, and safety objectives, while an environment-aware formation reward adjustment relaxes formation tracking near obstacles according to the distance to obstacle boundaries. Experiments under different obstacle densities and swarm sizes show that GDC-MASAC improves mission completion, collision avoidance, and formation coordination. In a scenario with 12 obstacles and 3 UAVs, GDC-MASAC achieves a mission success rate of 86%, whereas the baseline methods achieve success rates below 50%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of GDC-MASAC for cooperative multi-UAV path planning in cluttered environments.

radar.title: Group size effects and collective misalignment in LLM multi-agent systems
radar.venue_raw: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
radar.summary: Multi-agent systems of large language models (LLMs) are rapidly expanding across domains, introducing dynamics not captured by single-agent evaluations. Yet, existing work has mostly contrasted the behavior of a single agent with that of a collective of fixed size, leaving open a central question: How does group size shape dynamics? Here, we move beyond this dichotomy and systematically explore outcomes across the full range of group sizes. We focus on multi-agent misalignment, building on recent evidence that interacting LLMs playing a simple coordination game can generate collective biases absent in individual models. First, we show that collective bias is a deeper phenomenon than previously assessed: Interaction can amplify individual biases, introduce new ones, or override model-level preferences. Second, we demonstrate that group size affects the dynamics in a nonlinear way, revealing model-dependent dynamical regimes. Finally, we develop a mean-field analytical approach and show that, above a critical population size, simulations converge to deterministic predictions that expose the basins of attraction of competing equilibria. These findings establish group size as a key driver of multi-agent dynamics and highlight the need to consider population-level effects when deploying LLM-based systems at scale.

radar.title: Jointly Modeling Preferences and Imperfect Decision-Making in Large Language Models
radar.summary: Do preferences Large Language Models (LLMs) express in standard elicitation tasks predict their strategic behaviour? LLM agents interacting with humans and other AI systems face potentially conflicting objectives, such as individual welfare, group welfare, and environmental concerns. Prior work characterizes LLM preferences through behavioral-economic and psychological elicitation or strategic games, but rarely tests consistency across settings and prediction in other strategic environments. This requires modeling how competing objectives jointly shape behavior, whereas existing approaches typically measure preference dimensions in isolation. Drawing on utility theory, we introduce the Preference-Behavior Model (PBM), which combines a preference representation with mechanisms capturing imperfect utility maximization. We formulate estimation as an inverse-game problem, jointly inferring preferences and behavioral parameters from observed choices. We evaluate PBM in three social dilemmas that expose conflicting motives: a Public Goods Game, a Collective-Risk Dilemma, and a Common-Pool Resource dilemma. We find that while preferences estimated from established behavioral economic elicitation instruments do not consistently predict behavior in these dilemmas, models fitted in one dilemma retain predictive value in others, suggesting that inferred preferences capture meaningful aspects of LLM decision-making that elicitation instruments may miss. Finally, we assess alignment with persona instructions, finding that inferred preferences broadly reflect intended priorities with specific divergences across dimensions, LLMs, and games being identified by our approach. Our methodology provides a framework for studying how consistently LLM preferences explain behavior, assessing alignment with intended priorities, and revealing trade-offs and behavioral patterns that standard elicitation may miss.
